opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it starts with the problem rather than the technology. Materials discovery has historically been slow: you have an idea, synthesize something, characterize it, and often it doesn't work, so you loop again. That cycle can take years. What we're trying to do is compress that loop by turning it into a search problem in a very large space of possible materials, where AI helps decide where to look next.

So the platform is a layered system. At the bottom are physics-based simulations, things like density functional theory and molecular dynamics. They're accurate but expensive, so you can't run them on millions of candidates. On top of that we build machine learning surrogates, neural networks that learn to approximate those simulations at a fraction of the cost. Equivariant architectures matter a lot here, because you want the model to respect the symmetries of physics: rotate a molecule and the energy shouldn't change. Baking that in makes the models far more data-efficient, which matters when every training label costs real compute.

Then there's a generative layer. Instead of screening a fixed list, you want models that propose new structures conditioned on the properties you care about: a material that binds CO2 well, is stable, and is cheap to make. Diffusion-style generative models are well suited to that.

Wrapping all of that is what I'd call the decision layer: active learning and uncertainty quantification. The system should know what it doesn't know. When the surrogate is uncertain, you send that candidate to a more expensive simulation, or eventually to a lab, and feed the result back in. Being Bayesian about it, in the broad sense, is how you spend a limited budget of expensive experiments wisely.

The last piece is closing the loop with the physical world. Simulation alone won't get you there; synthesizability and real-world conditions always surprise you. So we design the platform to plug into experimental partners, so lab data continually corrects the models.

Philosophically, I see it as a kind of digital twin of the chemistry lab, a search engine for materials. The motivation is climate. We need better materials for carbon capture, batteries, and catalysts, and we need them on a timescale of years, not decades. If AI can shave a meaningful fraction off that discovery time, that's one of the most impactful things I can imagine working on.

r001.rationale: It describes cheap machine-learning surrogates screening candidates and sending selected uncertain candidates to more expensive simulations.

r002.rationale: It says experimental lab data feeds back to continually correct the models.

r003.rationale: It describes active learning and a decision layer, but does not identify autonomous agents as orchestrating computations and experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that we didn't start from the AI and look for a problem. We started from the problem, which is that discovering a new material is painfully slow and expensive, and asked where machine learning actually changes the economics. And the honest answer is that it changes them in a few specific places, not everywhere.

So the way I think about the platform is as a loop, not a model. You have a generative component that proposes candidate structures, you have a surrogate, a learned simulator, that estimates properties far faster than density functional theory or molecular dynamics would, and then you have the actual physics, the expensive simulation or ultimately the lab, as the ground truth you go back to. The intelligence is in how you close that loop: which candidates are worth paying for, where the model is uncertain, how you spend your compute and your wet-lab budget. That's really active learning and Bayesian decision-making dressed up in a modern wardrobe.

The second principle is that physics is not optional. These are molecules and crystals, and the laws don't care about your architecture. So equivariance, symmetries, conservation laws, those go into the model as inductive biases. I spent a lot of years on that, and the reason is simple: data in this domain is scarce and expensive, and every symmetry you bake in is data you don't have to collect. It also makes the predictions behave sensibly when you extrapolate, which in discovery you always are, because by definition you're looking for things that aren't in the training set.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that the platform has to be built for the chemists and the materials scientists, not for the ML engineers. If the output is a list of structures with no explanation of why, no uncertainty, no handle on what tradeoffs the model made, nobody in the lab trusts it, and rightly so. So a lot of the design is about making the uncertainty visible and making the loop something a domain expert can steer.

The thing I keep reminding the team is that the goal is not a better model. The goal is a material that exists and does something useful. If a dumber model gets you there faster because it fits the loop better, use the dumber model.

r001.rationale: It describes a fast surrogate screening candidates, then using expensive simulations or lab evaluations for candidates worth the cost.

r002.rationale: It says lab results provide ground truth that the discovery loop returns to, alongside active learning and Bayesian decision-making.

r003.rationale: The workflow is described as a loop guided by active learning and domain experts, but autonomous agents are not identified as its orchestrators.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a closed loop between proposing materials and learning from what happens when you test them. You start with the properties you want, and the model suggests candidates. Then you need to ask: Are they stable? Can we actually synthesize them? And do they have the properties we predicted?

So the platform needs to bring together generative models, physics-based simulation, and experiments. The results feed back into the model and help decide what to try next. Uncertainty is important here: sometimes the most useful experiment is one that teaches you something, rather than one that simply confirms your best prediction.

The goal is to make that whole cycle more efficient. Generating a structure is one step; getting to a material that you can make and use is the real challenge.

r001.rationale: It describes proposing and testing materials, but does not say that inexpensive screening narrows candidates before more expensive evaluations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says experimental results feed back into the model and help decide what to try next.

r003.rationale: It mentions models, simulations, and experiments, but does not identify autonomous agents as orchestrating the workflow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a closed loop. You have a model that proposes materials, you have simulations or experiments that tell you how those materials actually behave, and then you use that feedback to improve the model. The important thing is to design those pieces together.

You’re usually working backward: you know the properties you want, and you’re trying to find a structure or composition that delivers them. But predicting an interesting material is only part of the problem. Can you make it? Is it stable? Can you measure the property you care about? Those constraints need to enter the discovery process early.

And uncertainty matters enormously. You don’t just want the model to suggest what it thinks is best. You want it to help decide which experiment would be most useful next—sometimes to improve a candidate, sometimes to learn something that changes where you search.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulations or experiments in a feedback loop, but does not say that inexpensive screening narrows candidates before more expensive evaluations.

r002.rationale: It says simulations or experiments provide feedback that is used to improve the model, clearly communicating experimental results feeding back into discovery.

r003.rationale: It describes a model and a closed-loop workflow, but does not identify autonomous agents as orchestrating computations and experiments.
